query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A post-synthesis, mild thermal aging treatment in a low‐oxygen/water‐vapor atmosphere will induce a controlled surface segregation in the near‐equiatomic, multi‐principal‐element automotive alloy catalyst. This segregation forms a thin, protective high‐entropy oxide overlayer that is enriched in the minor platinum‐group elements, thereby simultaneously enhancing low‐temperature oxidation activity, resistance to H2O and NO poisoning, and long‐term durability without increasing overall precious metal loading.
generation.material_initial_state: A near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst containing a uniform solid solution of base metals with low loadings of platinum-group metals.
generation.intervention: Subject the catalyst to a controlled mild thermal aging treatment (e.g., around 700 °C for a limited time) in an atmosphere containing low partial pressures of O2 and H2O vapor.
generation.conditions: Simulated automotive exhaust conditions including transient, low-temperature (<150 °C) operation, exposure to water vapor (~10 vol%) and NO, and accelerated aging protocols that mimic the thermal and chemical stresses experienced over a vehicle lifetime.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, conformal high‐entropy oxide overlayer—selectively enriched in the platinum‐group elements—that covers the catalyst surface while leaving the bulk alloy near equiatomic.
generation.mechanism: The mild thermal treatment drives selective migration of the more oxidation‐resistant (and catalytically active) platinum‐group elements to the surface, where they form a protective, high‐entropy oxide layer. This overlayer improves active site binding energetics for low‐temperature oxidation, resists adsorption of poisoning species (H2O and NO), and retards sintering or structural degradation during prolonged operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the treated catalyst should achieve full conversion (T100) at temperatures below 150 °C, exhibit minimal deactivation when exposed to H2O and NO, and show significantly reduced performance losses over prolonged aging tests simulating real-driving conditions.
generation.baseline: The untreated near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst shows acceptable activity but is more sensitive to water/NO poisoning and more prone to sintering and degradation under long-term thermal exposure, leading to higher light-off temperatures and accelerated performance decline.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective only if the catalyst composition permits controlled surface segregation without disrupting the bulk near-equiatomic state; if the thermal treatment is too harsh or if the alloy lacks sufficient platinum-group content, the benefits may not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thermal treatment parameters (temperature, time, atmosphere) and the long-term stability of the resulting oxide overlayer under dynamic, real-world exhaust conditions remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element catalyst samples. Subject one set to the controlled mild thermal aging treatment in a low‐oxygen/water‐vapor atmosphere, while keeping the other set as an untreated control. Test both sets under simulated automotive exhaust conditions that include transient low-temperature operation (<150 °C), exposure to water vapor (~10 vol%) and NO, and accelerated aging cycles.
measurements: Light‐off temperatures (T50 and T100) for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Conversion rates in the presence of H2O and NO (to assess poisoning resistance)
Microstructural analysis (via TEM/SEM) to detect sintering and confirm the formation of a surface oxide overlayer
Surface composition analysis (via XPS) to verify enrichment of platinum‐group elements at the catalyst surface
Durability tests over extended aging cycles to monitor activity decay
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal aging treatment fails to produce a statistically significant reduction in light-off temperatures, does not enhance resistance to water and NO poisoning, or if surface analysis does not confirm the formation of an enriched protective oxide overlayer (with little or no improvement in long-term durability over the untreated catalyst), then the hypothesis shall be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: CO is an asphyxiating gas toxic to humans at concentrations exceeding 0.1%.[  ] The primary sources of CO emissions are motor vehicle exhaust and industrial flue gas, produced by the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels.[  ] Currently, the catalytic oxidation of CO is thought to be the most effective and energy‐efficient technique for purifying CO. The catalytic oxidation of CO is a key heterogeneous gas‐solid process and a valuable probe for studying catalyst structure, metal‒support interactions, adsorption‐desorption behavior, and reaction mechanisms.[  ] The catalytic activity, stability, and water tolerance of the Pt/HEO for CO oxidation were systematically evaluated. As shown in Figure 4a, the Pt/HEO catalyst achieved full CO conversion at 195 °C, significantly lower than the 430 °C required by HEO nanofibers alone (Figure S33, Supporting Information), highlighting the critical role of Pt nanoparticles. Interestingly, the catalytic performance of the Pt/HEO improved substantially after thermal aging. After aging in N2 at 700 °C, the conversion temperature dropped to 182 °C. cited_evidence.text: These results underline the exceptional thermal stability of Pt nanoparticles, which is attributed to the high‐entropy effect. As shown in Figure 4g, the Pt/HEO‐850 °C catalyst demonstrated excellent stability during CO oxidation at 210 °C, maintaining consistent activity over 338 h with ignorable decline (Table S3, Supporting Information). The Pt/HEO‐850 °C demonstrates a slight decline (2.4%) in the 30‐h running with a low deactivation rate constant (k d) of 3.2 × 10−3 h−1, compared with recent Pt‐based catalysts (Figure 4h).[  ] This result exceeds the thermal stability conventional catalysts, showcasing its superior sinter‐resistance. To simulate hydrothermal conditions, vapor was introduced during testing, and even after 35 consecutive cycles, ignorable performance declines were observed (Figure 4i). In the 36th cycle, the porous structure remained intact, with the Pt nanoparticle size increasing only by 0.1–2.7 nm (Figures S36 and S37, Supporting Information). The durability of Pt/HEO in moisture‐rich environments, such as automotive exhaust systems, underscores its potential as a highly reliable catalyst for CO oxidation.
